title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search
authors: Maria Ilektra Plakitsi, Sebastian Feld, Akash Kundu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS. At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's new discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.

infographic.key_insight: LatentRL-QAS enables transfer across qubit counts by reusing learned circuit representations in a shared latent space while keeping the RL agent’s dimensions fixed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Decoupling the RL agent from qubit count removes the need to enlarge its state, action space, and network when searching larger quantum circuits.
method: Encode circuits as one token per gate using a variational autoencoder with a shared latent space.
Train an RL agent to navigate latent representations rather than add gates directly.
Periodically refresh the representation with new discoveries and expand it for larger systems using smaller-system solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On five- and six-qubit absolutely maximally entangled state tasks, LatentRL-QAS succeeded in 89–99% of evaluation episodes; baseline RL-QAS found neither target under the same budget despite 10–17× larger networks.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer is demonstrated on AME-state preparation; its effectiveness and representation-refresh costs for broader circuit-design tasks remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search

title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
authors: Yixiong Chen
abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.

infographic.key_insight: QPAT uses a learnable quantum generative prior during classical model training, aiming to improve predictions while keeping inference entirely classical.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework integrates with LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers without requiring quantum hardware at inference time.
method: Use a Quantum Circuit Born Machine to supply a task-aligned, structured training prior.
Apply decoupled fitness-based scoring to guide prior learning.
Use stochastic Drop-Prior to implicitly distill quantum structure into classical weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six benchmarks in forecasting, vision, and NLP, the abstract reports better predictive performance and cross-seed stability than classical backbones, with ablations favoring QPAT over random and classically learned priors.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify quantum training costs or establish a computational advantage over classical alternatives.
infographic.paper_title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference

title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
authors: Sumit Choudhary, Tarunpreet Kaur, Harjeet Kaur, Harpreet Singh
abstract: Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound $Λ$-deuteron and $Λ$-$α$ hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

infographic.key_insight: Residual learning with convex projection improves quantum error mitigation while ensuring reconstructed density matrices remain physically valid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can improve noisy-hardware bound-state simulations, but training-state selection and regression-model choice affect accuracy.
method: Learn error corrections using residual regression, then apply convex projection to enforce density-matrix validity.
Evaluate Haar-random versus VQE-ansatz training states and different regression models.
Compare with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On IBM hardware, three-qubit Λ-deuteron simulations achieved −0.134 MeV versus an ideal −0.135 MeV with 0.999 fidelity; four-qubit Λ–α simulations achieved −3.014 and −3.045 MeV with fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover only three- and four-qubit systems; scalability and generalization beyond the evaluated training distributions remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations

title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation
authors: Norifumi Matsumoto, Yuya O. Nakagawa, Shota Kanasugi, Yuichiro Hidaka, Kazunori Maruyama, Hirotaka Oshima
abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.

infographic.key_insight: Directly estimating small energy-level differences with paired quantum evolutions lowers sampling cost by replacing the full-Hamiltonian norm scale with one tied to the Hamiltonian derivative and parameter shift.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce early fault-tolerant quantum computing resources for molecular forces, energy gradients, and response-property calculations.
method: Combine time evolution under the original and parameter-shifted Hamiltonians in one quantum circuit.
Use non-adaptive statistical sampling to reconstruct energy differences directly.
Jointly estimate energy eigenvalues and their differences to characterize the energy landscape.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations and resource estimates on prototypical systems, including the Fermi-Hubbard model, indicate reduced resource requirements without loss of precision.
infographic.watch_item: Practical savings depend on implementing both Hamiltonian evolutions accurately; the abstract reports simulations and resource estimates, not hardware demonstrations.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation

title: Reducing T gates in product formulas with agent loops
authors: Luis Mantilla Calderón, Jérôme F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Kohei Nakaji, Taylor L. Patti, Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Quantum chemistry calculations on a fault-tolerant quantum computer usually require many $\text{T}$ gates. This cost depends on the simulation method and how precisely its rotations are implemented. In this paper, we used Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a large language model (LLM), in a coding-agent loop to optimize the structure and rotation-synthesis precision of product formulas (PFs) for quantum phase estimation (QPE). Each of five independent searches optimized a shared protocol across 115 HamLib molecular Hamiltonians spanning 4--16 qubits over 100 code mutations. The searches started from a calibrated, nested second-order PF with uniform synthesis precision. We minimized $T_{95}$, the estimated total $\text{T}$-gate cost including QPE queries and repeated attempts for $95\%$ success probability, while requiring chemical accuracy for every training Hamiltonian. We name the best protocol found error-limited optimized Trotter evolution (ELOTE). It achieves chemical accuracy for its training data and achieved median and geometric-mean $T_{95}$ reductions of $85.35\%$ and $84.82\%$, respectively. ELOTE combines contributions to the same Pauli string, uses a first-order PF, and varies synthesis precision with coefficient magnitude, Pauli support, and diagonal character. We also tested ELOTE on 76 larger Hamiltonians with 18--22 qubits, which met chemical accuracy in every case. For ten reaction energies, we further optimized a shared $δ$-ELOTE protocol. It reduced geometric-mean $T_{95}$ by $58.90\%$ relative to ELOTE while preserving chemical accuracy for every signed reaction difference. These classically verified results show cost savings from shared protocols across molecules and reactions, and motivate similar searches in which energy measurements from quantum computers guide explorations in a coding-agent loop.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM coding-agent loop discovered ELOTE, a product-formula protocol that reduced median estimated T-gate cost by 85.35% while preserving chemical accuracy across 115 training molecular Hamiltonians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing product-formula structure and rotation-synthesis precision together could substantially lower fault-tolerant quantum chemistry resource requirements.
method: Run five independent agent searches, each with 100 code mutations, to optimize a shared protocol across molecules.
Minimize estimated T-gate cost for 95% success probability, subject to chemical accuracy for every training Hamiltonian.
Combine identical Pauli terms, use a first-order product formula, and tailor synthesis precision to coefficient magnitude, Pauli support, and diagonal character.
infographic.evidence_signal: Classical verification found chemical accuracy on all 115 training Hamiltonians (4–16 qubits) and 76 larger test Hamiltonians (18–22 qubits); a shared δ-ELOTE protocol for ten reaction energies cut geometric-mean cost a further 58.90% relative to ELOTE.
infographic.watch_item: Savings are classically verified resource estimates, not demonstrated quantum-hardware performance; applicability beyond the evaluated molecules and sizes remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Reducing T gates in product formulas with agent loops

title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations
authors: Masahiro Tadokoro, Tetsuo Kodera
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below $10^{-10}$ per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm $\times$ 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed dense silicon spin-qubit architecture combines surface-code memories, shuttling lanes, and routing junctions to support scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design connects logical storage and gate operations with semiconductor-compatible integration and multiplexed control wiring.
method: Store rotated surface-code logical qubits in memories supporting logical single-qubit operations.
Connect memories through one-dimensional spin-shuttling lanes and cross junctions implementing transversal logical CNOT gates.
Evaluate logical errors using demonstrated device parameters and estimate capacity under multiplexed wiring constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The analysis estimates that code distance ≥21 is needed for logical errors below 10⁻¹⁰ per syndrome cycle and projects over 120,000 logical qubits on a 100 mm × 100 mm chip with optimized wiring efficiency.
infographic.watch_item: These are architecture-level estimates, not a demonstrated integrated system; scaling depends on reliable shuttling, junction operations, and optimized control wiring.
infographic.paper_title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations

title: Search-for-Gradient: Search-Based Restarts for Optimisation in Structured Flat Landscapes of Variational Quantum Algorithms
authors: Subham Das, Bikash K. Behera, Andrés Camilo Granda Arango, Giuseppe Sergioli, Roberto Giuntini
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a promising class of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms that involve parameterised quantum circuits and classical optimisation. VQAs have found applications in simulation, optimisation, and machine learning. However, their scalability is hindered by flat landscapes-regions in the parameter space where gradients vanish exponentially small. In such regimes, gradient-based optimisation methods fail because parameter updates become ineffective in the absence of informative gradients. In this work, we propose a search-based restart framework to escape flat regions in structured flat landscapes, in which small trainable regions exist within a large flat landscape. This framework approaches the plateau escape as a search problem and locates trainable regions. The optimiser's parameters stop updating when the gradients vanish, and the method then searches over-sampled points to identify landscapes with nonzero gradients. We provide theoretical estimates of the number of jumps and the probability of escape from flat landscapes. This restarts the local optimisation process and avoids stagnation. We tested this framework on synthetic functions that mimic structured flat landscapes and a real quantum circuit cost landscape. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that Search-for-Gradient improves optimisation performance in structured flat landscapes. The proposed framework assumes the existence of a trainable region with nonzero measure and will not work if it has zero measure. Our framework can be integrated with existing VQAs to improve trainability and robustness.

infographic.key_insight: Search-for-Gradient restarts stalled optimisation by searching for trainable regions within otherwise flat variational quantum algorithm landscapes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can augment existing VQA optimisers to reduce stagnation when informative gradients exist elsewhere in parameter space.
method: Detect stalled parameter updates caused by vanishing gradients.
Search sampled parameter points for nonzero gradients.
Restart local optimisation in a discovered trainable region.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved optimisation on synthetic structured-flat functions and a quantum-circuit cost landscape, alongside theoretical estimates of jump counts and escape probability.
infographic.watch_item: The method requires a trainable region of nonzero measure and cannot escape if that region has zero measure.
infographic.paper_title: Search-for-Gradient: Search-Based Restarts for Optimisation in Structured Flat Landscapes of Variational Quantum Algorithms

title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Leyan Lyu, Shabnam Jabeen
abstract: While hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks (QCPINNs) are often described as efficient because they have fewer trainable parameters than classical PINNs, parameter count does not measure wall-clock cost. To examine this gap on a one-dimensional seawater temperature diffusion benchmark, with the quantum circuits simulated on a CPU, we time the four cumulative stages a PINN needs (the forward pass, the first- and second-order input gradients, and the PDE-loss parameter gradient) for a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations that differ in qubit count and circuit depth, and size-matched classical controls that share the hybrids' classical layers. We find that the hybrids are 14-56x slower than the classical PINN for the forward pass and 10-97x slower for the PDE-loss parameter gradient, and even against the size-matched controls, they remain 9-85x slower. Further, over the tested ranges, runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count, approximately linearly with circuit depth, and sub-linearly with batch size, while for the circuit-only forward pass, a second simulator backend was 10-165x slower under the same calling pattern. Although the hybrids have 38-44% fewer parameters than the classical PINN, this reduction comes from their smaller classical layers, as the quantum circuit accounts for at most 2.5% of each hybrid's parameters. Yet parameter count failed to predict runtime even among the classical networks, since the size-matched controls, despite having fewer parameters than the classical PINN, run slower than it. Our conclusion is that fewer parameters did not mean lower cost: every hybrid took at least ten times longer than the classical PINN at every stage, and the gap grew quickly with the number of qubits.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid quantum-classical PINNs had 38–44% fewer parameters but took at least 10× longer than the classical PINN at every measured stage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Benchmark wall-clock costs across forward passes and derivative computations rather than using parameter count as a proxy for computational efficiency.
method: Tested a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations, and size-matched classical controls on 1D seawater temperature diffusion.
Timed cumulative forward, first- and second-order input-gradient, and PDE-loss parameter-gradient stages with CPU-simulated quantum circuits.
Examined runtime scaling with qubit count, circuit depth, batch size, and simulator backend.
infographic.evidence_signal: Hybrids were 14–56× slower for forward passes and 10–97× slower for PDE-loss parameter gradients than the classical PINN, with approximately exponential runtime growth as qubit count increased over the tested range.
infographic.watch_item: These results concern a single diffusion benchmark with CPU-simulated circuits and do not establish runtime performance on quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
authors: Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik
abstract: Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

infographic.key_insight: Using higher-dimensional quantum units called qudits can increase information capacity per carrier and naturally encode high-dimensional systems for quantum simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Qudits offer a route to extracting more processing capability from a fixed number of physical carriers, provided their additional levels can be reliably controlled and measured.
method: Review experimental progress in qudit preparation, control, and measurement across five hardware platforms.
Survey early demonstrations of qudit-based simulation, computation, and error suppression.
Outline challenges and future directions for scalable qudit processing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports high-fidelity experimental progress and early application demonstrations, but provides no numerical benchmarks or comparative performance data.
infographic.watch_item: Higher information capacity does not eliminate decoherence or the need for fault tolerance, and scalable multilevel control remains a challenge.
infographic.paper_title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing

title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits
authors: Cenk Tüysüz, Simon Deconihout, Enrico Rinaldi, Michele Grossi
abstract: Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a $7\times7$ Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. Through classical circuit design, we demonstrate low-temperature state preparation at circuit sizes beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.

infographic.key_insight: PP-VarQITE determines thermal-state circuit parameters entirely classically, encoding temperature in the angles of a fixed, shallow quantum circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shallower circuits reduce quantum hardware execution demands and enable low-temperature state preparation beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.
method: Combine Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution.
Compute circuit parameters classically for different target temperatures.
Execute fixed-architecture circuits on trapped-ion quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies reached 100 qubits with circuits approximately 2–10× shallower than the lowest-depth sequential tensor-network compilations; Helios experiments used 96 and 98 qubits, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers.
infographic.watch_item: The reported benchmarks do not establish classical parameter-computation costs or accuracy for arbitrary models and lower temperatures.
infographic.paper_title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits

title: The integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition for nonlinear dynamics: Efficient Hamiltonian simulation of the Stepanoff flow
authors: Ilon Joseph, Ivan Novikau, Michael R. Montgomery, Joanna Slawinska, Dimitrios Giannakis
abstract: We propose an efficient unitary numerical time integration strategy for nonlinear dynamical systems: the integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition (I-LTS). First, express the generator as a sum of integrable parts. Second, approximate the full evolution operator using a Lie-Trotter-Suzuki (LTS) decomposition of the desired approximation order in time step. The I-LTS construction ensures that the full evolution operator can be represented as a product of terms that each have an efficient explicit tensor product factorization that can be handled efficiently with tensor network and/or quantum block-encoding methods. Next, we apply this method to an important non-integrable point example of a dynamical system: the Stepanoff flow on the torus. First, we derive an efficient unitary quantum algorithm for simulating the Stepanoff flow that can be thought of as a unitary classical version of a quantum map. Then, we provide a detailed description of the encoding of the two-dimensional system into an efficient quantum circuit, including an efficient block-encoding for all required operators. An efficient Hamiltonian simulation algorithm is constructed using a sequence of alternating quantum Fourier transforms (QFT) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) circuits. Finally, the circuit is simulated using a numerical emulator of fault-tolerant quantum computers, and the results are found to be consistent with several alternative classical computational methods. While efficient, the need for Trotterization introduces fundamental complexity in requiring small enough time step for an accurate approximation and solving for the transfer operator requires one to confront the linear scaling of the advection operator with grid size.

infographic.key_insight: Integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition enables efficient unitary simulation of nonlinear dynamics by splitting the evolution generator into integrable parts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach provides a structured route to implementing nonlinear dynamical simulations with tensor networks or quantum block-encoding methods.
method: Split the generator into integrable components with explicit tensor-product factorizations.
Approximate evolution using a Lie-Trotter-Suzuki product formula of the desired order.
Encode the Stepanoff flow on a torus using alternating quantum Fourier transform and quantum signal processing circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Fault-tolerant quantum circuit emulation produced results consistent with several alternative classical computational methods; the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy or speedup.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy requires sufficiently small Trotter steps, while the advection operator scales linearly with grid size, constraining simulation cost.
infographic.paper_title: The integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition for nonlinear dynamics: Efficient Hamiltonian simulation of the Stepanoff flow

title: A machine learning architecture for scaling of holographic quantum circuits
authors: Cliff Sun, Michael L. Wall
abstract: We describe an architecture and workflow for learning and generalizing the syntax and parameters of holographic quantum circuits (HQCs), which are natural quantum circuit analogs of classical tensor networks. An HQC uses mid-circuit measurements and resets on a small subset of "physical" qubits whose measurement outcomes become correlated through coupling with a register of persistent "ancilla" qubits, analogous to the physical and bond indices of a tensor network. Hence, an HQC with fixed qubit resources can efficiently generate samples from a large quantum state, and adding qubits to the HQC ansatz has the effect of exponentially increasing the effective bond dimension. Our machine learning approach provides mechanisms for harnessing both features of HQCs by extrapolating the syntax (e.g., a sequence of gates, measurements, and resets) and parameters (e.g., the angles appearing in single-qubit rotations) from a dataset of HQCs to longer or more expressive HQCs. We demonstrate the methodology and its performance on an analytically solvable dataset formed by a vector-valued generalization of the W-state. Finally, we provide an outlook for usage of the methodology for scaling the effective bond dimensions of HQCs in quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: A machine learning architecture learns holographic quantum circuit syntax and parameters to extrapolate toward longer or more expressive circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing measured and reset qubits enables sampling from large quantum states with fixed qubit resources, while additional persistent ancillas exponentially increase effective bond dimension.
method: Use physical qubits with mid-circuit measurements and resets, coupled to persistent ancillas.
Learn gate, measurement, and reset sequences alongside rotation parameters from circuit datasets.
Extrapolate learned syntax and parameters to scale circuit length or expressivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The methodology is demonstrated on an analytically solvable dataset based on a vector-valued generalization of the W-state; the abstract reports no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the solvable dataset and robustness to hardware noise remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A machine learning architecture for scaling of holographic quantum circuits

title: Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss
authors: J. Wilson Staples, Winston Fu, Yihe Dong, Jeff D. Thompson
abstract: Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, \texttt{slim}, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (Gross) code, we study a walking syndrome extraction circuit with Pauli and loss errors. For physical error rates $p<1\%$, we observe a more than $10^3$-fold lower logical error rate for a pure loss model, relative to a pure Pauli error model at the same physical error rate, along with significantly enhanced sub-threshold error rate scaling. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.

infographic.key_insight: A loss-aware CNN decoder turns qubit-loss information into substantially improved error correction, including for a high-rate qLDPC code.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast loss simulation and neural decoding offer a practical route to evaluating error correction for quantum hardware with detectable qubit loss.
method: Train loss-aware CNN decoders using the new slim sampler for circuits with Pauli noise and qubit loss.
Benchmark surface-code decoding against computationally expensive most-likely error decoders.
Evaluate a walking syndrome-extraction circuit for the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle (Gross) code.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulations, surface-code accuracy matches most-likely error decoding at much lower latency; for the Gross code at physical error rates below 1%, pure loss yields over 1,000× lower logical error rates than pure Pauli noise at the same rate.
infographic.watch_item: The largest reported gain compares idealized pure-noise models; hardware benefits will depend on mixed noise and reliable loss-resolving measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss

title: Native higher-order optimization with entropy quantum computing
authors: Narendra N. Hegade, Pranav Chandarana, Sebastian Wagner, Bahman Qawami, Wesley Dyk
abstract: Higher-order interactions are common in applied optimization: parity checks, radar-code sidelobes, portfolio skewness and kurtosis, and marketing-channel synergies all yield cubic or quartic objectives. Quantum annealers and most Ising machines accept only quadratic objectives, and gate-based quantum processors build every higher-order term from two-qubit gates. Entropy quantum computing, realized in the hybrid photonic-electronic Dirac-3S system, accepts polynomials of degree up to five with all-to-all coupling over binary, integer or simplex-constrained continuous variables. No user-supplied quadratization or circuit compilation is needed. We formulate four industrial use cases as six cubic and quartic instances, run them on Dirac-3S with 30 samples each, and score every sample against a certified optimum or a classical best-known value. We also estimate their cost on quantum annealers, superconducting grids and trapped-ion registers under standard mappings. For the two densest instances, a portfolio with about 80,000 terms and a budget allocation with 360,000 terms, the quadratized problems need embeddings far beyond current annealers, over $10^5$ physical qubits for the portfolio alone, and one phase-separation layer costs over $10^6$ two-qubit gates before optimization. Dirac-3S ran all six natively and returned feasible, distinct solutions. All samples of the binary instances are single-flip local minima. The best portfolio sample lies within 0.32% of the best-known value and the best budget sample 15% above it, but no sample reached its reference. Classical solvers reach the references within minutes at these sizes, and random starts followed by a local polish reach comparable or better values, so the advantage established here is one of expressibility and mapping cost, not of solution quality. Whether it extends to time to solution at larger sizes remains open.

infographic.key_insight: Dirac-3S solves higher-order optimization natively, demonstrating an expressibility and mapping-cost advantage—not superior solution quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Native polynomial support can avoid the auxiliary variables, embedding overhead and two-qubit gate counts required by conventional quantum mappings.
method: Formulated four industrial use cases as six cubic and quartic optimization instances.
Ran 30 samples per instance on the hybrid photonic-electronic Dirac-3S system.
Compared results with reference objectives and estimated mapping costs for annealers and gate-based processors.
infographic.evidence_signal: All six instances yielded feasible, distinct solutions; the best portfolio result was within 0.32% of its reference, while the best budget result was 15% above its reference.
infographic.watch_item: No sample reached its reference; classical solvers reached references within minutes, and larger-scale time-to-solution advantage remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Native higher-order optimization with entropy quantum computing

title: Empirical De-Quantization and Norm-Controlled Spectral Audit of Quantum Cognition Machine Learning in an Emerging Equity Market
authors: Pavel Chuklanov
abstract: Quantum-inspired machine learning in econophysics describes states of financial markets through matrix Hamiltonians, using ground-state expectations to predict returns and spectral gaps to identify crises. Although early work reports encouraging advances, it remains unclear whether these stem from genuine noncommutative quantum geometry or from conventional classical regularization and scale effects. We test this in a controlled audit of matrix-form Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML) and variational quantum circuits on the Moscow Exchange (2020-2025), combining daily equity data with causally lagged macro news under realistic trading costs, short-selling bans, and abrupt shifts in market regimes. By using capacity-matched operator swaps -- which progressively eliminate complex Berry phases and matrix noncommutativity down to a commuting classical Gibbs radial-basis limit under scale-invariant regularization -- as well as testing spectral indicators against radial-norm null hypotheses and untrained GUE random matrices, we isolate the contribution of each quantum element. In out-of-sample data, neither complex phases, noncommutativity, nor circuit entanglement improves the ranking of returns relative to classical controls. Once feature magnitudes are normalized, apparent crisis detection from raw spectral gaps drops below chance levels. These results show that on noisy equity panels, matrix-form QCML acts as an adaptive spectrally bounded classical smoothing kernel: it reliably integrates lagged news and curbs extreme crisis forecasts without passing economic multiple-testing thresholds, while our audit provides operator-swap and random-matrix controls for evaluating future quantum-inspired financial models.

infographic.key_insight: On Moscow Exchange equities, quantum-specific features offered no out-of-sample return-ranking advantage over classical controls, while matrix-form QCML behaved like a classical smoothing kernel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Benchmark quantum-inspired financial models against capacity-matched classical controls and normalize feature magnitudes before attributing gains to quantum structure.
method: Progressively removed complex phases and noncommutativity through capacity-matched operator swaps.
Audited spectral crisis indicators against radial-norm nulls and untrained random matrices.
Compared variational circuits and classical controls under trading costs and short-selling bans.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using Moscow Exchange daily equities from 2020–2025 with causally lagged macro news, out-of-sample tests found no advantage from phases, noncommutativity, or entanglement; magnitude normalization pushed spectral-gap crisis detection below chance.
infographic.watch_item: Results are specific to this noisy equity setting, and reported economic performance did not pass multiple-testing thresholds.
infographic.paper_title: Empirical De-Quantization and Norm-Controlled Spectral Audit of Quantum Cognition Machine Learning in an Emerging Equity Market

title: Amatlas: A 2D Array Architecture for Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination
authors: Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Seita Tsuboi, Hidetsugu Irie, Junichiro Kadomoto
abstract: Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.

infographic.key_insight: Amatlas maps Union-Find surface-code decoding onto a 2D processing-element array without a central controller or array-wide stage synchronization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Local neighbor links and per-stabilizer memory make the architecture better suited to planar hardware than a 3D processing-element array.
method: Assign one processing element to each stabilizer on the 2D qubit lattice.
Store measurement-round states in each element’s local memory.
Advance every element each clock cycle, with the clock as the only global signal.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation fits a VCU129 FPGA at code distance 25 and averages 462 ns per round at 0.1% physical error, with a 0.72% threshold versus 0.78% reported for Union-Find under the same noise model.
infographic.watch_item: Scaling beyond distance 25 remains un demonstrated here, and average latency alone does not establish worst-case real-time performance.
infographic.paper_title: Amatlas: A 2D Array Architecture for Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination

title: NISQ Preparation of Conditional Thermal States for Precision Thermometry
authors: Emery Doucet, Reece Robertson, Nicholas Donatelli, Shou-I Tang, Sebastian Deffner, Akira Sone
abstract: The ability to prepare thermal states on gate-based quantum computers is an important building block for quantum computation, both with regard to the implementation of certain classes of quantum algorithms as well as to the study of quantum thermodynamics in and out of equilibrium. A useful generalization of the standard notion of a thermal state which appears naturally in the study of quantum work distributions is the conditional thermal state, which is conditioned on the use of an accessible pointer basis associated with a measurement apparatus. Among other uses, it has been proven that conditional thermal states can outperform ordinary thermal states in quantum thermometry. In this work we demonstrate the preparation of conditional thermal states of few-qubit systems implemented on IonQ's cloud-based quantum computers across a range of temperatures. To validate their performance advantage in thermometry, we measure the sub-quantum Fisher information (a lower bound on the quantum Fisher information) of the prepared states, which can be computed via a constant-depth quantum circuit without tomography.

infographic.key_insight: Conditional thermal states offer a route to improved quantum thermometry and were prepared on few-qubit IonQ hardware across a range of temperatures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Preparing these states on gate-based quantum hardware supports practical exploration of precision thermometry and quantum thermodynamics.
method: Condition thermal states on an accessible measurement pointer basis.
Prepare few-qubit conditional thermal states on IonQ cloud quantum computers.
Measure sub-quantum Fisher information using a constant-depth circuit without tomography.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports hardware preparation across multiple temperatures and measurement of a lower bound on quantum Fisher information to evaluate thermometric performance.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstration is limited to few-qubit systems, and the abstract does not quantify the thermometric advantage or scalability under hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: NISQ Preparation of Conditional Thermal States for Precision Thermometry

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
authors: Masayuki Miyamoto
abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound. In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.

infographic.key_insight: A new quantum algorithm lowers the stated TSP time bound from O*(1.7274^n) to O*(1.70961^n) by combining extremal set systems with quantum search and dynamic programming.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a theoretical route to faster exact routing and related combinatorial optimization, though runtime remains exponential.
method: Split the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of unequal sizes.
Use extremal set systems and dynamic programming to compute subpath optima with small success probability.
Apply amplitude amplification within the quantum search framework.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical runtime and quantum space–time tradeoff improvements, plus matching bounds for related problems, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Practical value depends on quantum resource requirements and overheads not specified in the abstract; O* suppresses polynomial factors.
infographic.paper_title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More

title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
authors: Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz
abstract: Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

infographic.key_insight: The Blueprint proposes preparing DOE for fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment beginning in 2028, with scientific utility as the central goal.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Integrating fault-tolerant quantum computers into national scientific computing infrastructure requires programming expertise, system software, and facility readiness.
method: Target initial systems with at least 100 logical qubits and 10,000–100,000 hard logical operations per scientific calculation.
Develop FTQC programming capabilities, system software, and deployment infrastructure.
Invest in applications, algorithms, and logical architectures to enable larger production-scale systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites recent error-corrected logical-operation demonstrations and commercial hardware roadmaps as motivation, but reports no new benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The 2028 deployment goal and subsequent scaling to 1,000–10,000 logical qubits remain roadmap targets, not demonstrated capabilities.
infographic.paper_title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing

title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
authors: Xiaoran Li, Zhi Yin, Zhupeng Han, Zhengquan Pan, Kangyu Zheng
abstract: Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation. We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

infographic.key_insight: TyxonQ connects quantum chemistry solvers to multiscale classical workflows, enabling selected electronic subspaces to receive quantum treatment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its workflow interfaces support incremental quantum integration into existing chemistry simulations while retaining classical methods elsewhere.
method: Connect PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, backends, and classical consumers.
Combine QM/MM and fragment embedding with CCSD/FCI, variational, and sampling-based solvers.
Provide adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS through i-PI, and MDI.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation of correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support.
infographic.watch_item: Small-workflow evaluations do not establish industrial-scale performance or quantum advantage, and supported interfaces are not necessarily execution-tested.
infographic.paper_title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
